title: Big questions
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: V-NEUN GEO TURNS A CLAUSE INTO A THING. The doing of it — and then it takes ordinary particles, -ga to be a subject and -reul to be an object. Abstract talk is this one move, repeated.

ENGLISH HAS THREE SHAPES AND PICKS BY THE VERB. Gerund, infinitive, that-clause. Korean picks by the FRAME: -neun geo stands free, while -gi appears only inside the fixed frames L4-M1, L4-M2 and L4-M6 taught.

KOREAN BUILDS THE SENTENCE BACK TO FRONT. English puts the abstract noun first and modifies it afterwards — the freedom to choose. Korean puts the whole modifier before the noun, so you must know the ending before you begin.

N-(I)RANEUN GEO-SEUN OPENS A BIG QUESTION. The thing called X is... — written straight onto the noun with no hyphen, exactly as L5-M1 writes -raneun. English has no counterpart shorter than a whole clause.
-DAGO REPORTS A BELIEF WITHOUT QUOTING IT. jeo-neun ... -dago saenggakhaeyo is I think that... L3-M5's -rago quotes the words somebody said; -dago reports the thought behind them.
SARAM-MADA IS PER PERSON, NOT SOME PEOPLE. It says the thing varies with whoever you ask, and it is the ordinary way a values conversation opens without anybody having to be wrong.
THE WORD IS GACHIGWAN, NOT GACHI. gachi is L2-M6's together, and in this romanization the two are one and the same key. gachigwan is the word a conversation about values actually uses.
THIS MODULE HOLDS A BELIEF UP AND LOOKS AT IT. It does not defend one. A case made and an objection answered belong to L5-M6, and a question with no right answer is where this module stops.

words.note: The state rather than the mood — a life that is going well, not an afternoon that is. The k softens to g when a particle follows.
The predicate every big question ends on. jungyohan is the form that sits in front of a noun, and jungyohadago the one a reported belief takes.

sentences.trap: haengbok is the abstract noun, not the feeling of a good day. Korean keeps them apart, and this word belongs to the conversation about a whole life.

variations.changed: -eun for -i: happiness set up as the topic rather than claimed
a different value in the same frame

mistake.why: Written with a hard k where the sound has already softened. Once -i follows, the syllable is said haengbog-, and this course writes the romanization the way the word is said.

sentences.usage: The opening move of a conversation that is going to go somewhere.
sentences.mnemonic: Haengbog-i: the k goes soft before the particle.

words.note: The form a verb takes in front of geo. It is not a tense: it only says the clause is now attached to the noun that follows it.

sentences.trap: English can say living in Korea and stop. Korean cannot: -neun leaves the clause hanging until geo arrives to be the thing it describes, and only then can a particle attach.

variations.changed: -reul for -ga: the same clause as an object

variations.cue: How one lives is what matters.
variations.changed: the place dropped, the clause bare

mistake.why: A finished verb cannot take a particle. The clause has to become a thing first — saneun geo — and only that thing can be the subject of the sentence.

sentences.usage: Answering what is it like, with something more than fine.
sentences.mnemonic: Verb-neun geo, and now it is a noun.

sentences.cue: The thing called freedom really matters.

words.note: The value, and the first noun the definition frame is built on. -raneun is written straight onto it with no hyphen, exactly as L5-M1 writes it.
geo with the topic particle, and the second half of the definition frame. It sets the named thing up so that the rest of the sentence can say what it is.

sentences.trap: English has no short form of this. What we call freedom is four words to Korean's two, and a learner who drops the frame turns a definition back into an opinion.

variations.cue: The thing called happiness is different for each person.
variations.changed: a noun ending in a consonant, so -iraneun rather than -raneun
the plain claim, with the definition frame taken off

mistake.why: -raneun is an ending and not a particle, so it is written onto the noun with nothing between. Hyphenating it splits one word into two and leaves raneun standing on its own.

sentences.usage: Opening a question rather than answering one.
sentences.mnemonic: X-raneun geo-seun: the thing called X.

words.note: -mada is each, not some. It says the thing varies with whoever you ask, and nobody in the sentence is being told they are wrong.
What a person weighs things by, taken whole. The shorter gachi is L2-M6's together in this romanization, so this is the word to use.

sentences.trap: -mada is not some people. Some people think... invites a disagreement; saram-mada says the difference is simply the shape of the thing, which is a much softer way to open.

variations.changed: a different abstract noun in the same frame
the frame dropped, and the sentence is now about two people

mistake.why: This says some people have different values, which sets those people against the rest. saram-mada says every person has their own, and picks nobody out.

sentences.usage: Making room for a disagreement before it has happened.

words.note: A life taken as a whole span. The shorter sam shares its romanization with the number three here, so this course says insaeng and leaves sam unwritten.
Both dreams at once, as in English: the one you have asleep and the one you are working towards. Context decides, and nothing in the word does.

sentences.trap: Korean puts the modifier in front and English can put it either way, so jjalbeun has to be decided before kkum is reached. That is the whole difficulty of the module in four words.

variations.changed: -i for -eun: the claim rather than the topic being set
the other sense of the word, standing on its own

mistake.why: English can add the adjective afterwards for effect; Korean cannot. A modifier that arrives after its noun has arrived after the sentence has finished.

sentences.usage: The kind of thing said late in an evening, and meant.
sentences.mnemonic: The short comes before the dream.

sentences.cue: I think meaning is what matters.

words.note: What a thing is for, rather than what it means in a dictionary. It is the noun a big question keeps coming back to.

sentences.trap: -dago is not -rago. L3-M5's -rago repeats the words somebody used; -dago reports the thought, and only -dago can carry a belief of your own.

variations.cue: I think happiness is what matters.
variations.changed: a different value inside the same reported belief
the belief asserted flat, with nobody holding it

mistake.why: -rago quotes, so this reports somebody saying the words meaning matters out loud. A belief takes -dago on the stem: jungyohadago.

sentences.usage: Putting your own view into a conversation without closing it.

words.note: One verb for both English words. With a person it is trust, with a clause it is believe, and Korean never asks you to choose between them.

sentences.trap: English splits trust a person from believe a claim and Korean does not. The object decides which one an English translation needs, and the Korean is the same word either way.

variations.changed: the subject dropped, as Korean drops it by default
an abstract noun where English would have to say believe in

mistake.why: saenggakhaeyo is to think about, so this says you have your friend on your mind. Trust is mideoyo, and the two verbs are not near each other in Korean.

sentences.usage: Said plainly, and heard as a bigger claim than the English sounds.
sentences.mnemonic: One verb: trust and believe together.

sentences.cue: What people believe is different for each of them.

words.note: The noun made from mideoyo. It covers a religious faith and an ordinary trust between people, and the sentence around it decides which.

sentences.trap: This module names the frame and leaves the content out. mideum here is anybody's belief, and no sentence in the course says whose or what.

variations.changed: the noun as a subject, and a claim instead of an observation

variations.cue: Values are different for each person.
variations.changed: a different abstract noun in the same frame

mistake.why: teullyeoyo says wrong. Swapping it for dallayo turns an observation that beliefs vary into a claim that everybody else's is mistaken.

sentences.usage: Stepping back from a disagreement without settling it.

words.note: The world as people and how they live, not the planet. It is the subject a big question about change is usually built on.
byeonhaeyo in the shape that goes in front of geo. The whole clause in front of geo-reul is what mideoyo is believing.

sentences.trap: The believing verb comes last and the belief is built entirely in front of it. English starts with I believe and works forwards; here nothing is said until the clause is finished.

variations.cue: I think about how the world changes.
variations.changed: a different verb taking the same nominalised clause
the claim on its own, with nobody believing it

mistake.why: This is the English order transplanted. The verb closes a Korean sentence, and the clause it takes has to be finished before it arrives.

sentences.usage: The nearest thing to a creed this course will teach.

sentences.cue: That question has no right answer.

words.note: A question somebody asks, and the -e is to it rather than at it. It takes the particle even where English uses none.
Not any answer — the correct one, the one an exam has. Saying a question has none is a claim about the question, not about the asker.

sentences.trap: jeongdap is the right answer, not a reply. Saying there is no jeongdap does not refuse to answer; it says the question is not that kind of question.

variations.changed: the verdict with the question left out

variations.cue: Does that question have a right answer?
variations.changed: the whole thing asked rather than settled

mistake.why: Two topics in one sentence and nothing to hold them together. The question takes -e, to it, and jeongdap is the only thing the sentence is about.

sentences.usage: Closing a conversation that was never going to be settled, and meaning it kindly.
sentences.mnemonic: No jeongdap — and that is the answer.

comprehensionPool.cue: I think meaning is what matters.
What people believe differs from person to person.
That question has no right answer.
How one lives is what matters.
